To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there is a trend in the DNA sequences of eukaryotes and prokaryotes for (G/C)n (A/T)m(G/C)n to occur more frequently than (G/C)2n (A/T)m and (G/C)n+2(A/T)m, and that the twist and roll angles of DNA are correlated with these trends.
The DNA sequence pattern (G/C)n (A/T)m (G/C)n, where n and m are integers less than or equal 7, is preferred over the pattern (G/C)(n + 2) (A/T)m.
there is a trend in DNA sequences to have A/T blocks inserted inside G/C sequences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the structural and biological basis of sequence patterns in DNA.
the spatial aspects of the DNA structure and their relationship to DNA function.
the spatial arrangement of G/C blocks and A/T stretches in DNA, as observed in the GenBank data bank.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a preferred spatial arrangement in the DNA sequence.
the DNA sequence trends are related to the DNA structural properties, and that the latter in turn are related to the nucleosome formation.
the (A/T)n(G/C)2 arrangement is favored over (G/C)n(G/C) + 2(A)T)n.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the A/T stretches are positioned in the interior of G/C blocks, and this arrangement provides greater flexibility in the positioning of the G/T blocks.
the DNA sequence is arranged in such a manner as to maximize flexibility of the G/C blocks, and minimize the flexibility of the A/T blocks.
the DNA sequence patterns are influenced by the spatial considerations in the packaging and folding of the DNA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a preferred arrangement in the spatial positioning in eukaryotic DNA, which is in agreement with our previous findings on prokaryotic sequences.
the DNA sequence is not just an informational molecule, but also a highly flexible one.
DNA sequences have evolved with the constraint that their spatial arrangement in the cell nucleus is important.
